title: Nada
hook: John of the Cross: nothing, nothing, nothing, and on the mountain, nothing: letting go for love

segments.voice: Yesterday, Teresa's castle of clear crystal, room inside room. Your line was the king is in the center. When the courtyard got loud, did you step inward? Day one thousand one hundred thirty-six.

A small sketch, drawn by hand, of a mountain. At the bottom, paths split off. On the wrong roads, the drawing is labeled with the things people chase: having, knowing, comfort, glory. Up the narrow middle path, one word repeats, again and again, and near the top of the mountain, the same word once more. Nada. Nothing. The sketch was made by a Spanish Carmelite friar, Teresa's companion in reforming their order, known as John of the Cross. And the word on his mountain path sounds, at first, like a bleak word to put on a mountain. Today's word: nada.

Here's what John actually means, and it isn't despair. In his book The Ascent of Mount Carmel, he gives a set of short sayings that work like a riddle. To come to enjoy everything, desire to enjoy nothing. To come to possess everything, desire to possess nothing. To come to know everything, desire to know nothing. Nada is the price, and todo, everything, is the prize. The nothing is for the sake of the all. Why? John's picture is that a heart full of grasping has no room left. If your hands are clenched around a pile of small things, you can't receive the one great thing. So the nothing isn't hatred of the world. Mountains, rivers, the night air: John's poems are full of them. The nothing is about the grip. It's letting go of the clutch, the need to own, so that love has space. Paul says something close in his letter to the Philippians: "I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord." Not that everything is worthless. Just that next to the one thing, he can let the rest go. John isn't gentle about how hard this is. Letting go can feel like loss, like night. And yet his mountain is drawn going up. The narrow path of nothing is the one that reaches the top. On his sketch, near the summit, the word is nada again, and that's where he places God's honor and glory. In John's picture, empty hands at the top turn out to be full.
screen: `NADA IS THE PRICE, TODO THE PRIZE.`
`NOT HATRED OF THE WORLD, LOOSER GRIP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let go of one thing. Sit, and close one hand into a fist, firmly, and feel the grip. Ask what you're gripping right now. It might be an object, a plan, being right in an argument, an image of yourself. Pick just one. Don't throw it away in disgust. Slowly, a finger at a time, let the fist uncurl, and let your hold on that one thing loosen with it. If you pray, you can offer it to God as the hand opens. If you don't, just feel the difference between the grip and the release. The bell holds the time.
Nada. Spanish for nothing. In John of the Cross, the letting go that makes room for everything, for love.
Your line: nothing, for all. Today, when you catch yourself clutching, at a phone, a grudge, a plan, open the hand a little and see what fits in. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-six.

howItsDone: Carmelites and others who follow John of the Cross practice detachment, letting go of attachments to things, comforts and even spiritual feelings, so that the heart is free to love God; it is often taught with a spiritual director.

notes: The todo/nada sayings (Ascent I.13.11) are paraphrased, not quoted; confirm the three chosen (enjoy, possess, know) follow John's order closely enough.

The sketch of Mount Carmel: labels on the side paths (goods of earth: possessing, joy, knowledge, consolation, rest; goods of heaven: glory, joy, knowledge, consolation, rest) are simplified to 'having, knowing, comfort, glory'; the repeated 'nada' up the middle path and 'y aun en el monte nada' near the top; and the summit inscription about God's honor and glory. Confirm the description, especially 'that's where he places God's honor and glory'.
Claims rule: no count of 'nadas' is given; the outline's three/four is avoided on purpose.
Hook: 'Teresa's companion in reforming their order' is a general relation; confirm. 'People have called him the poet of the dark night' attributed; confirm or cut.
'John's poems are full of them' (mountains, rivers, the night air) draws on the Spiritual Canticle and The Dark Night; confirm.
Original: Greek ζημία (ζημίαν in Philippians 3:8), used because Spanish 'nada' is plain ASCII for the game; confirm accent and pronunciation.

Editor (2026-10-02): cut the unsourced epithet 'poet of the dark night'; cut the spoken gloss of zemia ('a forfeit, something handed over', a stretched word-meaning; the same 'Paul's Greek word for X' device also recurs on days 1139 and 1140), and changed the original note to 'loss, damage'; practice reworked from 'open hands on your knees' (repeated day 1126's posture) to a closed fist slowly uncurling.
Auditor (2026-10-02): the teach's last line ('empty hands... turn out to be full') asserted by the narrator; attributed to John's picture.
